6.1: The substance of the universe is obedient and compliant; and the reason which governs it has in itself no cause for doing evil, for it has no malice, nor does it do evil to anything, nor is anything harmed by it. But all things are made and brought to completion according to this reason.
6.2: Let it make no difference to you whether you are cold or warm, if you are doing your duty; and whether you are drowsy or have had enough sleep; and whether spoken ill of or praised; and whether dying or doing something else. For it is one of the acts of life, this act by which we die; it is enough, then, in this act too, to do well what we have in hand.
6.3: Look within. Let neither the particular quality of anything nor its value escape you.
6.4: All existing things soon change, and they will either be turned into vapour, if indeed all substance is one, or they will be scattered.
6.5: The reason which governs knows what its own disposition is, and what it does, and on what material it works.
6.6: The best way of taking revenge is not to become like the wrongdoer.
6.7: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: in passing from one social act to another social act, thinking of God.
6.8: The ruling principle is that which rouses and turns itself, and while it makes itself such as it is and such as it wishes to be, it also makes everything which happens appear to itself to be such as it wishes.
6.9: Every single thing is accomplished in keeping with the nature of the universe; for certainly it is not in keeping with any other nature that each thing is accomplished, whether a nature which contains this one from outside, or a nature which is contained within this nature, or a nature external to and independent of this one.
6.10: The universe is either a confusion, a mutual entanglement of things, and a scattering, or it is unity and order and providence. If, then, it is the former, why do I want to linger in a chance combination of things and such a disorder? And why do I care about anything other than how I shall at last become earth? And why am I disturbed, since the scattering of my elements will happen whatever I do? But if the other supposition is true, I revere, and I stand firm, and I trust in him who governs.
6.11: When you have been forced by circumstances to be disturbed in some way, quickly return to yourself, and do not stay out of tune longer than the compulsion lasts; for you will have more mastery over the harmony by continually returning to it.
6.12: If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would be dutiful to your stepmother, but still you would constantly return to your mother. Let the court and philosophy now be stepmother and mother to you: return to philosophy often and rest in her, through whom what you meet with at court seems bearable to you, and you seem bearable at court.
6.13: When we have meat before us and such things to eat, we take in the impression that this is the dead body of a fish, and this the dead body of a bird or a pig; and again, that this Falernian is only a little grape juice, and this purple robe some sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shellfish. Such, then, are these impressions, and they reach the things themselves and get right into them, and so we see what kind of things they are. In just the same way we ought to act all through life: where there are things which seem most worthy of our approval, we ought to lay them bare and look at their worthlessness, and strip them of all the words by which they are exalted. For outward show is a wonderful distorter of reason, and when you are most sure that you are busy with things worth your trouble, that is when it cheats you most. Consider, then, what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.
6.14: Most of the things which the multitude admire belong to objects of the most general kind, those which are held together by cohesion or natural organisation, such as stones, wood, fig trees, vines, olives. But those which are admired by men who are a little more reasonable belong to the things which are held together by a living principle, such as flocks and herds. Those which are admired by men who are still better educated are the things which are held together by a rational soul—not, however, a universal soul, but rational in so far as it is a soul skilled in some craft, or expert in some other way, or simply rational in so far as it owns a number of slaves. But he who values a rational soul, a soul that is universal and fitted for political life, regards nothing else except this; and above all things he keeps his soul in a condition and an activity in keeping with reason and social life, and he works together to this end with those who are of the same kind as himself.
6.15: Some things are hurrying into existence, and others are hurrying out of it; and of what is coming into existence, part is already extinguished. Motions and changes are continually renewing the world, just as the unbroken course of time is always renewing the infinite duration of ages. In this flowing stream, then, in which nothing stays, which of the things that hurry by would a man set a high price on? It would be just as if a man should fall in love with one of the sparrows flying past, when it has already passed out of sight. Something of this kind is the very life of every man, like the exhalation of the blood and the breathing in of the air. For just as it is to have once drawn in the air and given it back, which we do every moment, so it is with the whole power of breathing, which you received at your birth yesterday or the day before, to give it back to the element from which you first drew it.
6.16: Neither is transpiration, as in plants, a thing to be valued, nor breathing, as in domesticated animals and wild beasts, nor receiving impressions from the appearances of things, nor being moved by desires like puppets by strings, nor gathering in herds, nor being nourished by food; for this is just like the act of separating and getting rid of the useless part of our food. What, then, is worth valuing? To be received with clapping of hands? No. Nor must we value the clapping of tongues; for the praise which comes from the many is a clapping of tongues. Suppose, then, that you have given up this worthless thing called fame: what remains that is worth valuing? This, in my opinion: to move yourself and to restrain yourself in keeping with your proper constitution, the end to which all occupations and arts lead. For every craft aims at this, that the thing which has been made should be suited to the work for which it has been made; and the vine-planter who looks after the vine, and the horse-breaker, and he who trains the dog, all seek this end. But the education and teaching of the young aim at something. In this, then, lies the value of education and teaching. And if this is well, you will not look for anything else. Will you not stop valuing many other things too? Then you will be neither free, nor sufficient for your own happiness, nor free from passion. For you will necessarily be envious, jealous, and suspicious of those who can take those things away, and you will plot against those who have what you value. A man who lacks any of these things must necessarily be in a state of complete turmoil; and besides, he must often find fault with the gods. But to revere and honour your own mind will make you content with yourself, in harmony with society, and in agreement with the gods, that is, praising all that they give and have ordered.
6.17: Above, below, all around are the movements of the elements. But the motion of virtue is in none of these: it is something more divine, and, advancing by a way hardly noticed, it goes happily on its road.
6.18: How strangely men act! They will not praise those who are living at the same time and living with them; but to be praised themselves by posterity, by those whom they have never seen and never will see, this they set great value on. But this is very much the same as if you were to be upset because those who lived before you did not praise you.
6.19: If a thing is difficult for you to accomplish, do not think that it is impossible for man; but if anything is possible for man and in keeping with his nature, think that you can attain it too.
6.20: In the gymnasium, suppose that a man has scratched you with his nails, and by butting against your head has given you a wound. Well, we show no signs of annoyance, nor are we offended, nor do we suspect him afterwards of being a treacherous fellow; and yet we are on our guard against him, though not as an enemy, nor with suspicion, but we quietly get out of his way. Let your behaviour be something like this in all the other parts of life; let us overlook many things in those who are like opponents in the gymnasium. For it is in our power, as I said, to get out of the way, and to have neither suspicion nor hatred.
6.21: If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act rightly, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth, by which no man was ever harmed. But he is harmed who persists in his error and ignorance.
6.22: I do my duty: other things do not trouble me; for they are either things without life, or things without reason, or things that have wandered off and do not know the way.
6.23: As for the animals which have no reason, and generally all things and objects, since you have reason and they have none, make use of them with a generous and open spirit. But towards human beings, since they have reason, behave in a social spirit. And on all occasions call on the gods, and do not trouble yourself about how long you will spend doing this; for even three hours spent like this are enough.
6.24: Alexander the Macedonian and his groom were brought by death to the same state; for either they were taken back into the same seed-principles of the universe, or they were alike scattered among the atoms.
6.25: Consider how many things take place in each of us in the same indivisible moment—things which concern the body and things which concern the soul—and so you will not wonder if many more things, or rather all things which come into existence in that which is the one and all, which we call Cosmos, exist in it at the same time.
6.26: If anyone should put to you the question of how the name Antoninus is spelt, would you strain your voice and shout out each letter? What then if they grow angry, will you be angry too? Will you not go on calmly and count out every letter? Just so, then, in this life too, remember that every duty is made up of certain parts. It is your duty to observe these, and without being disturbed or showing anger towards those who are angry with you, to go on your way and finish what is set before you.
6.27: How cruel it is not to allow men to strive after the things which seem to them suitable to their nature and profitable! And yet in a way you do not allow them to do this when you are annoyed because they do wrong. For they are certainly drawn towards things because they suppose them to be suitable to their nature and profitable to them. But it is not so. Teach them, then, and show them, without being angry.
6.28: Death is a ceasing of the impressions through the senses, and of the pulling of the strings which move the appetites, and of the wandering movements of the thoughts, and of the service to the flesh.
6.29: It is a shame for the soul to be the first to give way in this life, when your body does not give way.
6.30: Take care that you are not made into a Caesar, that you are not dyed with this dye; for such things happen. Keep yourself, then, simple, good, pure, serious, free from affectation, a friend of justice, a worshipper of the gods, kind, affectionate, energetic in all proper acts. Strive to remain the kind of man philosophy wanted to make you. Revere the gods, and help men. Life is short. There is only one fruit of this earthly life—a pious disposition and social acts. Do everything as a disciple of Antoninus. Remember his constancy in every act that was in keeping with reason, and his evenness in all things, and his piety, and the serenity of his face, and his sweetness, and his disregard of empty fame, and his efforts to understand things; and how he would never let anything pass without first examining it most carefully and understanding it clearly; and how he put up with those who blamed him unjustly without blaming them in return; how he did nothing in a hurry; and how he would not listen to slander, and how exact an examiner of manners and actions he was; and that he was not given to reproaching people, nor timid, nor suspicious, nor a sophist; and with how little he was satisfied, such as lodging, bed, clothing, food, servants; and how hard-working and patient he was; and how, because of his sparing diet, he was able to hold out until the evening, not even needing to relieve himself except at the usual hour; and his firmness and consistency in his friendships; and how he tolerated freedom of speech in those who opposed his opinions; and the pleasure he took when any man showed him something better; and how religious he was without superstition. Imitate all this, so that you may have as good a conscience, when your last hour comes, as he had.
6.31: Come back to your sober senses and call yourself back; and when you have woken from sleep and seen that it was only dreams that troubled you, now in your waking hours look at the things around you as you looked at the dreams.
6.32: I consist of a little body and a soul. Now to this little body all things are indifferent, for it is not able to perceive differences. But to the understanding only those things are indifferent which are not the works of its own activity. But whatever things are the works of its own activity, all these are in its power. And of these, however, only those which are done with reference to the present; for as to the future and past activities of the mind, even these are for the present indifferent.
6.33: Neither the labour which the hand does nor that of the foot is contrary to nature, so long as the foot does the foot's work and the hand the hand's. So then neither is a man's labour, to him as a man, contrary to nature, so long as it does the things of a man. And if the labour is not contrary to his nature, neither is it an evil to him.
6.34: How many pleasures have been enjoyed by robbers, parricides, tyrants.
6.35: Do you not see how craftsmen accommodate themselves up to a point to those who are not skilled in their craft—but nevertheless they hold on to the principles of their art, and will not bear to depart from them? Is it not strange if the architect and the physician have more respect for the principles of their own arts than man has for his own reason, which he shares with the gods?
6.36: Asia and Europe are corners of the universe; the whole sea a drop in the universe; Athos a little clod of the universe; all the present time is a point in eternity. All things are little, changeable, perishable. All things come from there, from that universal ruling power, either directly or as a consequence. And so the lion's gaping jaws, and what is poisonous, and every harmful thing, such as a thorn or mud, are by-products of the grand and beautiful. Do not then imagine that they are of a different kind from what you revere, but form a just opinion of the source of all.
6.37: He who has seen present things has seen all, both everything which has taken place from all eternity and everything which will be for time without end; for all things are of one kin and of one form.
6.38: Often consider the connection of all things in the universe and their relation to one another. For in a way all things are bound up with one another, and in this way all are friendly to one another; for one thing comes in order after another, and this is because of the active movement and the working together and the unity of the substance.
6.39: Adapt yourself to the things among which your lot has been cast; and the men among whom you have received your portion, love them, but do it sincerely.
6.40: Every instrument, tool, vessel, if it does what it has been made for, is well, and yet the one who made it is not there. But in the things which are held together by nature the power which made them is within, and stays in them; and so it is all the more fitting to revere this power, and to think that, if you live and act according to its will, everything in you is in keeping with intelligence. And in this way also in the universe the things which belong to it are in keeping with intelligence.
6.41: Whatever thing not in your power you suppose to be good or evil for you, it must necessarily follow that, if such a bad thing happens to you, or you lose such a good thing, you will not blame the gods, and hate men too, those who are the cause of the misfortune or the loss, or those who are suspected of being likely to be the cause; and indeed we do much injustice because we do not treat these things as indifferent. But if we judge only those things which are in our power to be good or bad, there is no reason left either for finding fault with God or for taking a hostile stance towards man.
6.42: We are all working together towards one end, some with knowledge and design, and others without knowing what they do; as men do also when they are asleep, of whom it is Heraclitus, I think, who says that they are labourers and fellow-workers in the things which take place in the universe. But men work together in different ways: and even those work together abundantly who find fault with what happens and those who try to oppose it and prevent it; for the universe had need even of such men as these. It remains, then, for you to understand among what kind of workmen you place yourself; for he who rules all things will certainly make right use of you, and he will receive you among some part of the fellow-workers and of those whose labours lead to one end. But do not be such a part as the mean and ridiculous line in the play, which Chrysippus speaks of.
6.43: Does the sun take on the work of the rain, or Aesculapius the work of the Fruit-bearer, the earth? And how is it with each of the stars—are they not different, and yet they work together to the same end?
6.44: If the gods have made decisions about me and about the things which must happen to me, they have decided well, for it is not easy even to imagine a deity without forethought; and as for doing me harm, why should they have any desire for that? For what advantage would come from this to them or to the whole, which is the special object of their providence? But if they have not made decisions about me individually, they have certainly made them about the whole at least, and the things which happen as a consequence in this general arrangement I ought to accept with pleasure and be content with. But if they decide about nothing—which it is wicked to believe, or if we do believe it, let us neither sacrifice nor pray nor swear by them, nor do anything else which we do as if the gods were present and lived with us—but if, however, the gods decide about none of the things which concern us, I am able to decide about myself, and I can inquire into what is useful; and what is useful to every man is what is in keeping with his own constitution and nature. But my nature is rational and social; and my city and country, so far as I am Antoninus, is Rome, but so far as I am a man, it is the world. The things, then, which are useful to these cities are alone useful to me.
6.45: Whatever happens to each man is in the interest of the universal: this might be enough. But further, you will observe this also as a general truth, if you do observe, that whatever is profitable to any man is profitable also to other men. But let the word profitable be taken here in the common sense, as said of things of the middle kind, neither good nor bad.
6.46: Just as it happens to you in the amphitheatre and such places that the continual sight of the same things, and the sameness, make the spectacle tiresome, so it is in the whole of life; for all things above and below are the same and from the same. How long, then?
6.47: Think continually that all kinds of men, of all kinds of pursuits and of all nations, are dead, so that your thoughts come down even to Philistion and Phoebus and Origanion. Now turn your thoughts to the other kinds of men. To that place, then, we must move, where there are so many great orators, and so many noble philosophers, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates; so many heroes of former days, and so many generals after them, and tyrants; besides these, Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes, and other men of sharp natural talents, great minds, lovers of labour, versatile, confident, mockers even of the perishable and short-lived life of man, such as Menippus and those like him. As for all these, consider that they have long been in the dust. What harm, then, is this to them; and what to those whose names are entirely unknown? One thing here is worth a great deal: to pass your life in truth and justice, with a kindly disposition even towards liars and unjust men.
6.48: When you want to cheer yourself, think of the virtues of those who live with you; for instance, the energy of one, and the modesty of another, and the generosity of a third, and some other good quality of a fourth. For nothing delights so much as the examples of the virtues, when they are shown in the characters of those who live with us and present themselves in abundance, as far as possible. So we must keep them before us.
6.49: You are not dissatisfied, I suppose, because you weigh only so many litrae and not three hundred. Do not be dissatisfied, then, that you must live only so many years and not more; for just as you are satisfied with the amount of substance which has been assigned to you, so be content with the time.
6.50: Let us try to persuade men. But act even against their will, when the principles of justice lead that way. If, however, any man stands in your way by using force, turn to contentment and tranquillity, and at the same time use the obstacle for the exercise of some other virtue; and remember that your attempt was made conditionally, that you did not want to do the impossible. What, then, did you want?—Some such effort as this.—But you achieve your aim, even if the things you were moved towards are not accomplished.
6.51: He who loves fame considers another man's activity to be his own good; and he who loves pleasure, his own sensations; but he who has understanding considers his own acts to be his own good.
6.52: It is in our power to have no opinion about a thing, and not to be disturbed in our soul; for things themselves have no natural power to form our judgements.
6.53: Get into the habit of paying careful attention to what is said by another, and as far as possible, get inside the speaker's mind.
6.54: What is not good for the swarm is not good for the bee either.
6.55: If sailors abused the helmsman, or the sick the doctor, would they listen to anybody else? Or how could the helmsman secure the safety of those on the ship, or the doctor the health of those he attends?
6.56: How many of those with whom I came into the world have already gone out of it.
6.57: To the jaundiced honey tastes bitter, and to those bitten by mad dogs water causes fear; and to little children the ball is a fine thing. Why then am I angry? Do you think that a false opinion has less power than the bile in the jaundiced or the poison in someone bitten by a mad dog?
6.58: No man will stop you from living according to the reason of your own nature: nothing will happen to you contrary to the reason of the universal nature.
6.59: What kind of people are those whom men wish to please, and for what ends, and by what kind of acts? How soon will time cover all things, and how many it has covered already.
